European Journal of Haematology

REVIEW OPEN ACCESS

Light Chain Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance: Diagnosis, Biology, and Clinical Management

Sigurður Yngvi Kristinsson1,2 | Thórir Einarsson Long3,4 | Sigrún Thorsteinsdóttir1,5

1Faculty of Medicine, University of Iceland, Reykjavik, Iceland | 2Landspitali University Hospital, Reykjavik, Iceland | 3Department of Nephrology, Skåne University Hospital, Lund, Sweden | 4Department of Clinical Sciences, Lund University, Lund, Sweden | 5Department of Hematology, Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen University Hospital, Copenhagen, Denmark

Correspondence: Sigurður Yngvi Kristinsson (sigyngvi@hi.is)

Received: 25 May 2026 | Revised: 16 June 2026 | Accepted: 18 June 2026

ABSTRACT Light chain monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (LC-­MGUS) is defined by an abnormal serum free light chain ratio and elevated involved light chain in the absence of a detectable immunoglobulin heavy chain on immunofixation and of end-­organ damage attributable to a plasma cell disorder. It is the least characterized of the MGUS subtypes and the one whose accurate diagnosis is most dependent on the precision of the reference intervals used to interpret free light chain measurements. Population-­based screening has demonstrated that standard reference intervals substantially overdiagnose LC-­ MGUS through three independent mechanisms: age-­related physiological free light chain elevation, impaired renal clearance in chronic kidney disease, and ancestry-­related differences in individuals of African descent. Revised age-­stratified and kidney function–adjusted reference intervals reduce LC-­MGUS prevalence by 82%, with no observed progressions among reclassified individuals during available follow-­up of 4.6 years and have been validated across multiple independent international cohorts. For individuals of African ancestry, ancestry-­adjusted reference intervals provide a further essential and independent correction. True LC-­MGUS progresses along two biologically distinct trajectories: clonal expansion toward light chain multiple myeloma and toxic light chain misfolding toward AL amyloidosis. These pathways differ fundamentally in biology, determinants of progression, and clinical consequences. Risk models designed to predict myeloma progression incompletely capture the risk of amyloidogenic transformation. Because amyloidogenic transformation can occur in the setting of low clonal burden and only modestly abnormal free light chain levels, clinical evaluation must independently and explicitly address both trajectories at every patient encounter.

1 | Introduction

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is subclassified into IgM MGUS, non-­IgM MGUS, and light chain MGUS (LC-­MGUS) on the basis of the immunoglobulin class secreted by the clonal plasma cells [1]. LC-­MGUS differs fundamentally from the other subtypes because it is defined entirely by quantitative serum free light chain (FLC) testing, an abnormal FLC ratio in conjunction with an elevated involved light chain, in the absence of immunoglobulin heavy chain expression on immunofixation [2, 3].

LC-­MGUS is the precursor to two biologically distinct diseases [1, 3, 4]. Light chain multiple myeloma (LC-­MM) arises through progressive clonal expansion causing end-­organ damage through tumor mass and light chain toxicity [1]. AL amyloidosis arises through the intrinsic amyloidogenic properties of the secreted monoclonal light chain, leading to misfolding, fibril formation, and toxic deposition in organs such as the heart, kidneys, liver, and peripheral nerves [4]. These pathways differ fundamentally in biology, clinical features, and prognostic determinants, a duality that shapes LC-­MGUS management (Figure 1).

FIGURE 1 | Dual biologic progression pathways in LC-­MGUS.

Among the three MGUS subtypes, LC-­MGUS has been the least studied and may be particularly susceptible to diagnostic misclassification. Because it carries no serologically detectable M protein on standard electrophoresis, it is identified solely through quantitative FLC assay interpretation, and any inaccuracy in the reference intervals used propagates directly into false diagnosis. The clinical consequences of overdiagnosis are not trivial: unnecessary bone marrow biopsies, imaging investigations, patient anxiety, and surveillance burden to individuals who do not have a clonal disorder. Conversely, the clinical consequence of underdiagnosis, particularly failure to identify early AL amyloidosis, can be severe. Accurate reference intervals therefore have important implications for both diagnostic precision and patient management.

Large population-­based screening data have shown that standard FLC reference intervals misclassify a substantial proportion of individuals [5, 6]. Revised reference intervals markedly reduce false-­positive classification, with no progressions observed among reclassified individuals during available follow-­up; though longer-­term data are needed.

2 | Definition and History

LC-­MGUS is defined by an abnormal serum FLC ratio and elevated involved light chain, in the absence of heavy chain

expression on immunofixation and of end-­organ damage attributable to a plasma cell disorder [1, 3]. Kyle and Greipp first described idiopathic Bence Jones proteinuria as a distinct premalignant entity in 1982, recognizing that isolated light chain secretion in the absence of overt myeloma represented a clinically meaningful precursor state [7]. The development of a nephelometric serum FLC assay by Bradwell and colleagues in 2001 [8] provided the analytical foundation for the FLC reference intervals, which was derived from 282 healthy blood donors [2].

Dispenzieri and colleagues formally characterized LC-­MGUS epidemiology in a landmark 2010 study of 18,357 Olmsted County residents aged 50 and older: prevalence was 0.8%, annual progression rate approximately 0.3%, and 23% had coexistent renal disease, anticipating the importance of renal function as a confounder [3]. Kidney function-­specific reference intervals were subsequently established from a large population screening cohort, with eGFR-­stratified upper ratio limits of 2.62 (eGFR 45– 59), 3.38 (eGFR 30–44), and 3.30 (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73m2), reducing LC-­MGUS prevalence among individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) from 7% to 0.5% (Table 1) [5].

Recent population-­based studies have enabled refinement of FLC reference intervals, particularly through the large iStopMM screening cohort, which included 41,882 participants with normal kidney function from the iStopMM study,

published in 2025 [6]. Kappa FLC levels increased substantially with age even with preserved renal function, and 17.5% of values were falsely elevated by standard intervals. Age-­ stratified intervals were established: ratio 0.44–2.16 for those under 70 years, 0.46–2.59 for those 70 and older. Applying these reduced LC-­MGUS prevalence from 1.54% to 0.27%, an 82% reduction (Figure 2) [6]. The magnitude of this reduction relative to the 2010 Olmsted County estimate likely reflects differences in cohort composition, including the broader age distribution in the iStopMM cohort and the 23% prevalence of coexisting renal disease in the earlier cohort, which may have inflated FLC values. Importantly, among 1006 reclassified individuals, no progressions were observed over 4648 patient-­years, supporting the clinical safety, though median follow-­up of 4.6 years is relatively short and longer-­term data are required.

2.1 | External Validation

The iStopMM Freelite intervals have been independently validated across multiple populations. Across these studies, individuals reclassified as normal using revised reference intervals consistently demonstrated low progression risk, while those remaining abnormal retained elevated risk. Consistent findings have been reported in Danish [9], Israeli [10], Lebanese [11], and Chinese CKD [12] cohorts. Furthermore, the revised intervals have also been shown to improve risk stratification in heavy chain MGUS [13]. Finally, in an Italian amyloidosis cohort, the revised ratio preserved full diagnostic sensitivity for AL amyloidosis while reducing false-­positive findings in ATTR patients [14]. Recent American Society of Hematology guidance on AL amyloidosis discusses the utility of kidney-­specific FLC reference intervals and highlights the need for further validation in diverse populations [15].

3 | Analytical Considerations in FLC Testing

The evidence base for LC-­MGUS, the iStopMM reference intervals, and the IMWG diagnostic threshold, predominantly derives from studies using the Freelite assay (The Binding Site). The Siemens N Latex FLC assay and Sebia FLC assay yield systematically different numeric distributions and are not interchangeable with Freelite. Freelite produces higher absolute kappa FLC values and higher kappa-­to-­lambda ratios than N Latex, with a bias of approximately +31% for the ratio; the IMWG myeloma-­defining threshold of iFLC/niFLC ≥ 100 with Freelite corresponds to approximately ≥ 50 with N Latex [16, 17]. Concordance is lowest in the mildly abnormal range defining LC-­MGUS, in one study, 19 of 38 patients with abnormal Freelite ratios had normal N Latex ratios, all with values between 1.67 and 3.37 [18]. Whether this represents Freelite overdiagnosis or N Latex underdiagnosis cannot be determined without population-­based outcome data using N Latex. Limited real-­world data have documented clinically consequential discordance between Freelite and N Latex assays, including cases in which disease detected by Freelite was not identified by N Latex, resulting in delayed diagnosis of plasma cell leukemia and permanent hemodialysis. In one cohort, all five clinically significant discordant cases involved N Latex failing to detect disease identified by Freelite, with no clinically relevant failures observed in the reverse direction [16–18]. All reference intervals and thresholds in this review apply to Freelite. Clinicians must apply assay-­specific intervals, state the platform in all clinical communications, and not transfer thresholds across platforms without independent validation.

4 | Epidemiology

Under revised reference intervals, LC-­MGUS prevalence in adults with normal renal function is approximately 0.27%, rising from 0.18% in those aged 40–49 years to 0.41% in those aged 80 and older (Figure 2). Male sex is associated with approximately twice the prevalence of female sex (0.36% versus 0.19%) [6]. These prevalence figures are substantially lower than those derived from Katzmann intervals and represent the best current estimate of true clonal LC-­MGUS frequency in the population.

The overall prevalence of approximately 0.27% in adults aged 40 and older implies that LC-­ MGUS is present in hundreds of thousands of individuals in any large country. In Iceland, where the iStopMM study screened more than 75,000 individuals, representing over half the adult population aged 40 and older, the revised prevalence data have directly informed national clinical practice and provided the most granular population-­level FLC distribution data available [19].

4.1 | Racial, Ethnic, and Sex Differences

Racial differences in monoclonal gammopathy prevalence have long been recognized, with Black individuals showing approximately twofold higher rates of conventional MGUS compared with White individuals [20]. Bertamini et al. studied 10 035 individuals from three prospective cohorts, PROMISE US, PROMISE South Africa, and the Mass General Brigham Biobank, with 44% self-­identifying as Black [21]. Using Katzmann intervals, 14.8% of Black Americans and 27.8% of South Africans were diagnosed with LC-­MGUS, with 99% of cases kappa-­restricted, biologically implausible given the approximately 3:1 kappa-­to-­lambda distribution in overt LC-­ MM, suggesting that a great majority of these diagnoses likely reflected physiological variation rather than clonal disease. This elevation was independent of renal function, age, and sex, confirmed by genetic ancestry analysis. Ancestry-­ adjusted reference ranges were derived: kappa 7.97–77.50 mg/L, lambda 6.20–49.20 mg/L, FLC ratio 0.686–2.10. Applying these reduced LC-­ MGUS prevalence from 14.8% to 0.8% in Black Americans and from 27.8% to 2.8% in South Africans [21]. Three independent sources of overdiagnosis now have evidence-­ based corrections: age (iStopMM age-­stratified intervals), renal impairment (iStopMM CKD intervals), and African ancestry (Bertamini et al. ancestry-­adjusted intervals; Table 1). All three should be applied appropriately before LC-­MGUS is diagnosed.

5 | Differential Diagnosis of Abnormal FLC Results

Because LC-­MGUS is defined entirely by a quantitative laboratory measurement, distinguishing true clonal FLC abnormalities from physiological or reactive elevations is a practical imperative at every clinical encounter. Several common conditions produce FLC ratio abnormalities that mimic LC-­MGUS and should be systematically excluded before diagnosis [22].

Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia arising from chronic inflammatory conditions, autoimmune disease, chronic infection, or liver disease typically produces symmetric elevation of both kappa and lambda FLC with preservation or only modest distortion of the ratio. Clinical context, review of serum protein electrophoresis, and repeat testing after treatment of the underlying condition will generally resolve the picture [5].

Renal impairment is the most important confounder. Because free light chains are cleared by glomerular filtration and catabolized in the proximal tubule, reduced renal function elevates both kappa and lambda FLC, but preferentially kappa, because kappa chains circulate as monomers and are more dependent on renal clearance than lambda dimers [23]. This produces a

systematic upward shift in the kappa-­to-­lambda ratio entirely unrelated to clonal kappa production. This leads primarily to overdiagnosis of kappa LC-­MGUS but could also lead to under detection of small lambda clones that can be of importance such as in AL amyloidosis or monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (MGRS). Application of eGFR-­stratified reference intervals is recommended in any patient with CKD, and failure to apply them is the most common source of false-­positive LC-­ MGUS diagnosis in general practice [5]. While this systematic shift is well-­characterized for polyclonal-­based assays, it has been reported to occur to a lesser degree with the monoclonal-­ based Siemens N Latex assay [24]. However, it remains debated whether this reflects superior analytical specificity or a compensatory interference by uremic toxins in the lambda measurement [25].

African ancestry independently elevates the kappa-­to-­lambda ratio through a genetic mechanism that is distinct from renal function, age, sex, or comorbidity. Without ancestry-­adjusted reference intervals, the overwhelming majority of apparent LC-­ MGUS diagnoses in individuals of African descent represent overdiagnosis, as demonstrated by the near-­complete kappa restriction and implausibly high population prevalence seen with standard intervals [21].

Transient FLC ratio abnormalities may occur during acute illness, during hematological recovery following stem cell transplantation, or with certain biological therapies including checkpoint inhibitors and CAR-­T cell therapy [26]. Repeat testing after clinical stabilization is appropriate before concluding that LC-­MGUS is present.

Finally, LC-­MGUS is specifically defined by the absence of an intact immunoglobulin heavy chain on immunofixation [1].

6 | Natural History: Divergent Biologic Trajectories

The natural history of LC-­MGUS is defined by two biologically distinct trajectories: clonal expansion leading to LC-­MM, and toxic light chain misfolding leading to AL amyloidosis (Figure 1). These pathways differ in pathogenesis, clinical features, and prognostic determinants, and recognition of this divergence is central to clinical management.

The annual progression rate has historically been estimated at approximately 0.3%, lower than the 1% annual risk in conventional MGUS [3]. Two LC-­MGUS cohorts using the revised diagnostic criteria have been described showing a higher risk of progression over time than for individuals fulfilling the original criteria [9, 10]. In the Israeli cohort a total of 8 (7.7%) out of 104 patients progressed during follow-­up; progression to AL amyloidosis was not reported. In the Danish cohort, 21 of 191 individuals (9.8%) progressed over a median follow-­up of 3.7 years, including progression to MM (5.1%), AL amyloidosis (3.3%), and NHL (2%), corresponding to a 2-­ and 5-­year cumulative incidence of 5.8% and 8.9% and an annual progression rate of 3%. Despite limited sample size and follow-­up, these findings suggest a higher progression risk under revised compared with original diagnostic criteria.

A premalignant MGUS stage consistently precedes multiple myeloma in prospective studies, detectable years before clinical diagnosis [27]. Risk models developed for conventional MGUS primarily predict myeloma progression and incompletely capture AL amyloidosis risk; both pathways should be considered independently at each clinical encounter.

6.1 | Risk Factors of Progression

A high FLC ratio and immunoparesis have previously been identified as risk factors of progression in LC-­MGUS [10, 28]. Furthermore, in the previously mentioned Danish LC-­MGUS cohort, individuals with lambda LC-­MGUS had a significantly higher risk of progression compared to those with kappa LC-­ MGUS with an HR of 2.51 (95% CI: 1.01-­6.20). When progression to MM alone was considered, the estimate still indicated a higher risk associated with having lambda LC-­MGUS [9].

6.2 | Pathway 1: Clonal Expansion to LC-­MM

Progression follows the general paradigm of plasma cell disorders, with secondary genomic events accumulating within the clonal population and driving progressive marrow infiltration, rising FLC levels, and end-­organ damage. Recently, revised diagnostic criteria for light chain smoldering multiple myeloma (LC-­SMM) were established based on data from the screened iStopMM cohort and external validation in the nationwide Danish DALY-­CARE cohort [29]. LC-­SMM was defined by abnormal serum free light chain values, absence of detectable intact immunoglobulin by serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation, and 10% to 60% bone marrow plasma cell involvement in the absence of myeloma defining events. Individuals fulfilling these criteria had an annual progression risk of approximately 6%, increasing to approximately 9% among those with intermediate or high risk features according to the 2/20/20 model. LC-­SMM therefore represents a distinct precursor state with substantially higher progression risk than LC-­MGUS and warrants specialist evaluation and closer surveillance [1, 29]. FLC ratio magnitude is clinically informative within LC-­MGUS: in a flow cytometry sub-­study of iStopMM, clonal plasma cells were identified in 53.6% of LC-­MGUS cases, and 5.6% of those with kappa-­involved ratios above 3.15 progressed during a median follow-­up of 55 months versus none with ratios between 1.65 and 3.15 [30]. Ratio magnitude reflects underlying clonal burden and is not simply a binary abnormality; mildly abnormal ratios carry a very low near-­term risk of myeloma progression. Probability-­based prediction tools allow individualized estimation of the likelihood of 10% or greater marrow involvement using readily available laboratory parameters, enabling probability-­guided decision-­ making rather than reflexive bone marrow biopsy [31].

6.3 | Pathway 2: Amyloidogenic Transformation to AL Amyloidosis

In contrast to myeloma progression, amyloidogenic transformation does not require substantial clonal expansion. Bone marrow plasma cell involvement at AL amyloidosis diagnosis

is frequently below 10%; circulating FLC concentrations may be only modestly elevated. The pathological driver is the intrinsic amyloidogenic properties of the secreted light chain rather than tumor mass, organ damage is caused not by plasma cell infiltration but by the direct toxic effects of misfolded light chain fibrils on the myocardium, glomerulus, autonomic ganglia, and other target tissues [4]. Delays in diagnosis remain common, with median delays of 2.7 years from symptom onset [32]. Cardiac involvement is the principal determinant of outcome, with 5-­ and 10-­year overall survival of 43% and 27%, respectively, in a 40-­year cohort, and substantially worse outcomes with advanced cardiac disease at diagnosis, although survival has improved in the daratumumab era [33]. Delayed diagnosis contributes to irreversible myocardial injury and poorer outcomes. Bone marrow–based risk models do not capture amyloidogenic transformation, and patients with low predicted marrow plasma cell burden may still be at risk if the secreted light chain is amyloidogenic. This distinction is further illustrated by the recently described LC-­SMM cohort, in which progression to AL amyloidosis occurred despite the entity being primarily defined and risk stratified according to myeloma progression risk [29].

6.4 | Distinct Progression Determinants

For LC-­MM, risk correlates with FLC ratio magnitude, rising involved FLC levels, marrow burden, and cytogenetic features. For AL amyloidosis, risk is more closely related to intrinsic light chain properties. Monoclonal light chain glycosylation, detectable by MASS-­FIX testing on routine serum samples, is associated with a 20-­year AL amyloidosis progression rate of 21% versus 3.5% in those without glycosylation, independent of standard MGUS risk factors [34]. This finding reinforces the concept that amyloidogenic transformation is driven by biochemical features of the secreted protein rather than clonal mass, and mandates explicitly distinct surveillance strategies for each pathway.

7 | Pathogenesis

The pathogenesis of LC-­MGUS as a distinct entity remains incompletely characterized, and most available data derive from studies of LC-­MM and AL amyloidosis conducted in cohorts defined by inaccurate reference intervals that almost certainly included a substantial proportion of false-­positive cases. Data from non-­White populations are nearly absent, and future biological studies in cohorts defined by revised diagnostic criteria will be required to characterize the true molecular landscape of LC-­MGUS.

The molecular features of LC-­MGUS itself remain incompletely defined, as most genomic studies have focused on overt plasma cell malignancies. The absence of immunoglobulin heavy chain expression results in most cases from the absence of a functional productive IgH rearrangement at the DNA level rather than from failed rearrangement itself, a molecular distinction with implications for understanding clonal architecture [35]. in conventional myeloma, while hyperdiploidy is markedly less frequent (11% versus 30%), suggesting that t(11;14) defines a biologically distinct subset with particular amyloidogenic potential [36, 37]. Whether t(11;14) is present at the LC-­MGUS stage and what prognostic significance that may have remains unknown.

Sequence homology between circulating free light chain dimers and tissue-­deposited light chains confirms the circulating monoclonal FLC as the direct amyloid precursor [38]. Amyloidogenic potential appears to be encoded in part in germline variable domain gene segments; certain IGKV and IGLV gene families are overrepresented in AL amyloidosis relative to their prevalence in myeloma, meaning the progression pathway of a given LC-­MGUS clone may be partly determined at the level of the B cell progenitor from which it arose. This implies that the biochemical properties of the secreted protein, not simply the degree of clonal expansion, are the primary determinant of amyloidogenic risk, and that some clones may carry an intrinsic predisposition to the amyloidogenic pathway regardless of their proliferative tempo.

8 | Risk Stratification and Clinical Evaluation

Management of LC-­MGUS is guided by two independent but complementary objectives: identifying patients at risk for progression toward LC-­MM and detecting early organ involvement suggestive of AL amyloidosis. The tumor expansion pathway is typically gradual and detectable through laboratory evolution; the amyloidosis pathway may present insidiously with modest laboratory abnormalities yet carry a greater risk of irreversible organ failure if unrecognized. These objectives are not interchangeable, addressing one does not fulfill the other. The proposed clinical approach is summarized in Figure 3.

8.1 | Step 1: Confirming the Diagnosis (Figure 3)

Age-­ and kidney function-­stratified Freelite reference intervals should be applied (Table 1). An online calculator is available to assist with classification (https://​istop​mm.​com/​lcmgus/​). For individuals of African ancestry with normal renal function, ancestry-­adjusted intervals should be used [21]. Serum immunofixation must confirm absence of an intact heavy chain. Borderline or unexpected results should be repeated before further evaluation proceeds, a single mildly abnormal FLC ratio in the context of acute illness, renal impairment, or African ancestry should not trigger an immediate diagnostic workup without confirmatory testing.

8.2 | Step 2: Estimating Marrow Plasma Cell Burden

Once LC-­MGUS is confirmed, the probability of significant bone marrow plasma cell involvement should be estimated using the iStopMM multivariable prediction model (https://​ istop​mm.​com/​riskm​odel/)​ [31]. This tool, which has been externally validated in ethnically diverse populations [39], incorporates FLC ratio magnitude, absolute involved FLC

level, and other readily available parameters to generate an individualized probability of 10% or greater marrow plasma cells. Biopsy should be considered when this probability exceeds approximately 15% in patients under 60, or 20% in older patients, subject to clinical judgment, frailty, and life expectancy. A kappa-­involved ratio above 3.15 identifies a subgroup in whom clonal plasma cells are likely present and in whom more thorough evaluation is warranted [30]. If SMM or myeloma is identified, management should follow established guidelines.

8.3 | Step 3: Evaluating for AL Amyloidosis

Assessment for AL amyloidosis must proceed independently of marrow risk estimation; low marrow plasma cell burden does not exclude amyloidogenic transformation [15]. Baseline evaluation should include NT-­proBNP, high-­sensitivity troponin, quantitative urine protein, and creatinine with eGFR in all patients with confirmed LC-­MGUS, regardless of FLC ratio magnitude. The degree of FLC elevation does not reliably correlate with the severity of organ involvement, and the absence of marked laboratory progression should not reassure clinicians in the presence of compatible clinical features.

8.3.1 | The following organ-­specific findings should prompt urgent evaluation for AL amyloidosis

Cardiac: unexplained dyspnea, edema, or reduced exercise tolerance; heart failure with preserved ejection fraction; left ventricular hypertrophy unexplained by long-­term hypertension; low voltage on ECG or discordance between ECG voltage and wall thickness; disproportionately elevated NT-­proBNP or high-­ sensitivity troponin.

Renal: new or worsening proteinuria, particularly nephrotic-­ range (renal impairment may occur even in the absence of proteinuria due to interstitial or vascular amyloid deposition); intolerance to ACE inhibitors or ARBs prescribed for antiproteinuric therapy because of hypotension related to cardiac or autonomic involvement; or unexplained hypotension on previously tolerated antihypertensives.

Neurological: unexplained peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy; autonomic dysfunction including orthostatic hypotension or gastroparesis; bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome with cardiac disease.

Hepatic and gastrointestinal: unexplained hepatomegaly; cholestatic alkaline phosphatase elevation; unexplained diarrhea or weight loss.

Other: easy bruising or bleeding disproportionate to cause; acquired factor X deficiency from amyloid adsorption, although uncommon, should prompt immediate evaluation; macroglossia; periorbital purpura.

biopsy should be considered when cardiac involvement is strongly suspected and surrogate biopsies are negative. Congo red staining should be added to bone marrow biopsies in patients with smoldering or active myeloma to detect concurrent silent AL amyloidosis. Bone scintigraphy (PYP/DPD/HMDP) is not appropriate in suspected AL amyloidosis with a known plasma cell disorder, as tracer uptake is typically absent and may lead to misclassification. It should be reserved for ATTR amyloidosis after exclusion of a plasma cell disorder [15].

9 | Management and Follow-­Up

No treatment is indicated for LC-­MGUS in the absence of progression to smoldering myeloma, myeloma, or AL amyloidosis.

The goals of management are accurate initial diagnosis using appropriate reference intervals, longitudinal monitoring for clonal evolution, and systematic surveillance for early organ involvement along the amyloidosis pathway.

Baseline evaluation should include a full blood count, serum creatinine and eGFR, serum calcium, NT-­proBNP, high-­ sensitivity troponin, quantitative urine protein, and serum and urine immunofixation. Imaging is not required in patients with low bone marrow probability and no clinical features suggesting myeloma.

Laboratory evaluation, FLC, full blood count, creatinine, and calcium, should be repeated at 6 months to establish trajectory, using the same assay platform as the baseline measurement.

This initial 6-­month reassessment is important: stable results substantially reduce near-­term concern, while early laboratory evolution or emergence of new symptoms changes the management priority. Switching assay platforms during follow-­up invalidates trend analysis and may result in spurious apparent change or missed true progression; platform consistency throughout a patient's clinical course is critical for accurate interpretation.

For lower-­risk patients with a confirmed stable LC-­MGUS and no clinical features of AL amyloidosis, annual review incorporating FLC measurement, full blood count, renal function, urinary albumin or protein excretion (ACR, PCR, or equivalent quantitative urine protein measurement), calcium, NT-­proBNP, high-­sensitivity troponin, and clinical reassessment for organ involvement symptoms is appropriate. Annual assessment of urinary albumin or protein excretion (ACR, PCR, or equivalent quantitative urine protein measurement) may be particularly useful, as early renal AL amyloidosis can develop despite only modest changes in serum FLC parameters. Rising involved FLC levels, increasing ratio distortion, new proteinuria, new cardiac biomarker elevation, or any new clinical concern should prompt earlier reassessment and a formal re-­evaluation of both pathways. At every follow-­up visit, clinicians should revisit both the laboratory trajectory for myeloma progression and the clinical picture for evolving amyloidosis; these objectives are complementary but not interchangeable. Follow-­up intervals may be individualized based on patient age, comorbidities, and competing mortality risk.

If AL amyloidosis is confirmed, prompt referral to a specialist center with experience in systemic amyloidosis is essential. Survival is determined by cardiac stage at diagnosis, and delays in referral translate directly into worse outcomes.

Population-­based screening for LC-­MGUS is not currently recommended outside clinical trials; the iStopMM randomized controlled trial is evaluating whether systematic screening of the general population for monoclonal gammopathy improves overall survival, with results anticipated in future years [19].

10 | Conclusions

LC-­MGUS is a biologically distinct MGUS subtype whose accurate diagnosis depends on correct interpretation of serum free light chain measurements. Standard reference intervals overdiagnose LC-­MGUS through three independent mechanisms: age-­ related FLC elevation, renal impairment, and ancestry-­related variation. Revised reference intervals reduce prevalence by 82%, with no observed progression among reclassified individuals, and have been validated across multiple independent cohorts.

True LC-­MGUS progresses along two fundamentally distinct biological pathways, clonal expansion to myeloma and amyloidogenic transformation to AL amyloidosis, with direct implications for clinical management. Risk models predicting myeloma progression do not capture amyloidosis risk, and a low marrow plasma cell probability should not reassure clinicians in the presence of potential organ involvement. Clinical evaluation must explicitly address both trajectories, combining probability-­ based marrow assessment with systematic screening for AL

amyloidosis. Key questions remain, including the long-­term safety of revised reference intervals, the need for cross-­platform harmonization of FLC measurements, and the biological determinants of divergent progression pathways. Emerging genomic and proteomic approaches may refine risk stratification and improve early detection of clinically significant disease.
